# Brubru

> Brubru is an AI-powered strategic advocacy assistant for EU policy professionals. Its motto is "All the EU, with AI." — every feature widens EU coverage or makes it more accessible through AI. Brubru combines a conversational AI that narrates EU policy with a personalised monitoring cockpit and specialised legislative tools, so users can analyse policies, track every file moving through Brussels, draft amendments, check compliance, and act. Developed by Beresol BV.

Brubru serves EU policy professionals, lobbyists, advocacy organisations, think tanks, government agencies, law firms specialising in EU law, and academic researchers in EU studies. The platform is available at https://brubru.beresol.eu in six languages (English, Spanish, French, Italian, Dutch, Catalan) and offers four subscription plans (Starter, Advocate, Professional, EP) with a 14-day free trial. Custom Enterprise contracts are available on request.

## Features

Brubru is organised into six canonical products:

- [My EU Bubble](https://brubru.beresol.eu/my-eu-bubble): the personalised EU-monitoring cockpit and the post-login home — a static visualisation of everything Brubru tracks, in a four-section workspace. Start here: Overview, Policy Interests, My Documents, and News (EU institutional news plus what the whole Brussels advocacy ecosystem is publishing). Legislative Monitoring: tracked files, My Official Journal, amendments, a multi-law Comparator, the Commission Legislative Train Schedule, and EP committee + plenary votes. Institutional Monitoring: EU Calendar, AI committee transcripts, Council Watch, MEP Watch, plenary order of business, parliamentary questions, EC public consultations, and lobby meetings. Analysis & Strategy: cross-institution Position Analysis, AI legislative Predictions, Brubru data libraries, Research & Evidence, Stakeholder Mapping, and Strategy Docs.
- [Brubru Chat](https://brubru.beresol.eu/main): the AI conversational interface that explains the EU — what Brubru is, what it holds, and where any policy file stands — grounded in 40+ EU institutional sources and 300+ knowledge guides, answering in six languages with clickable links to the exact document and the relevant Brubru tool.
- [Amendator](https://brubru.beresol.eu/amendator): legislative amendment authoring in Akoma Ntoso XML, with AI-assisted drafting and export to XML, HTML, PDF and Word.
- [EU Law Comply](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eulawcomply): automated compliance gap analysis against EU-law obligation clusters, with actionable recommendations and exportable reports.
- [Tenderator](https://brubru.beresol.eu/tenderator): EU public-procurement and funding intelligence over TED notices, with AI matching and bid-readiness analysis.
- [Brubru Public Data API](https://brubru.beresol.eu/api): a paid REST API over Brubru's EU legal and institutional data — 8,710 laws, OJ publications, OEIL procedures, the Council register, the EU Who-is-Who, and the Publications Office / data.europa.eu surfaces — billed via prepaid micro-credits.

Additional capabilities: AI document generation (position papers, MEP briefings, talking points, and more) inside My EU Bubble; AI legislative-outcome Predictions (timeline, EP plenary vote, Council QMV, resolution leading indicators); and a growing public library of EU legislation machine-translated into Catalan at https://brubru.beresol.eu/legislacio-ue-catala/.

## EU Data Sources

- [EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/): Official Journal, adopted legislation, Commission proposals via RSS and SPARQL
- [European Parliament OEIL](https://oeil.secure.europarl.europa.eu/): Legislative Observatory procedure tracking via XML feeds
- [European Parliament Legislative Train](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/): Legislative Train Schedule with 500+ procedure files
- [EP Committee Work](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/committees/): Work in progress from all 26 EP committees
- [Have Your Say Portal](https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/): EC public consultations and roadmaps
- [EC Register of Documents](https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/documents-register/): Commission documents (COM, SWD, SEC, OJ) and College tentative agendas
- [EPRS](https://epthinktank.eu/): European Parliament Research Service briefings and studies
- [Council of the EU register](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/documents-publications/public-register/): Council, European Council and Eurogroup meetings, outcomes and documents
- [EU Transparency Register](https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/registre-de-transparence/): interest representatives, declared lobbying, and Commission/EP meetings
- [TED (Tenders Electronic Daily)](https://ted.europa.eu/): EU public-procurement notices, powering Tenderator
- [Publications Office / data.europa.eu](https://data.europa.eu/): the EU open-data portal, Cellar SPARQL, EU Vocabularies, Who-is-Who, CORDIS and general publications
- [STOA, JRC and Council ART](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/stoa/): scientific foresight, science-for-policy and strategic research feeds

## EU Canon (public explainers)

The EU Canon is Brubru's growing library of plain-language deep-dives on binding EU laws. Each page synthesises a single regulation or directive into an article-by-article explainer with glossary, family tree, official-source links, and structured-data (JSON-LD Legislation) for indexing. Aimed at non-specialists who want to understand a specific EU law in plain English without wading through EUR-Lex. Available in six languages: English, Spanish, French, Italian, Dutch, Catalan.

- [EU Canon library (root)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/): Index page listing every published canon entry. Start here when browsing.
- [Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR, Regulation (EU) No 575/2013)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2013-575_crr/index.html): EU implementation of Basel III for credit institutions and investment firms. Own funds, capital ratios (CET1 4.5%, Tier 1 6%, Total 8%), credit risk Standardised + IRB, large exposures, liquidity (LCR, NSFR), leverage ratio, Pillar 3 disclosure, SME Supporting Factor 0.7619. Full lineage Basel I to CRR III (Basel IV).
- [China BEV Countervailing Duties (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2754)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2024-2754_china_bev_duties/index.html): EU's first major countervailing-duty action of the green-transition era. Definitive additional duties on Chinese battery electric vehicles (CN ex 8703 80 10): BYD 17.0%, Geely 18.8%, SAIC 35.3%, Tesla (Shanghai) 7.8%, other cooperating 20.7%, all others 35.3%, on top of the 6.5% conventional MFN customs duty. Threat-of-injury finding under Article 8(8) of Reg (EU) 2016/1037. All 5 undertaking offers rejected. 5-year duration to 31 October 2029.
- [China and Egypt GFF Countervailing Duties (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/776)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2020-776_china_egypt_glass_fibre/index.html): Landmark anti-subsidy case on woven and stitched glass fibre fabrics (CN ex 7019 39 00 / 40 00 / 59 00 / 90 00). Definitive countervailing duties on China (CNBM Group 30.7%, Yuntianhua 17.0%, others 24.8% to 30.7%) and Egypt (Jushi Egypt and Hengshi Egypt 10.9%). First EU case to attribute Chinese government subsidies to Egypt-located production via the China-Egypt Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone (SETC-Zone) using Article 11 of the ILC Articles on State Responsibility (acknowledgement and adoption doctrine). Adopted 12 June 2020 (OJ L 189/1, 15.6.2020). Combined CVD plus AD: up to 99.7% for CNBM Group.
- [India and Indonesia Stainless Steel Countervailing Duties (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/433)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2022-433_india_indonesia_stainless_steel/index.html): Anti-subsidy case on stainless steel cold-rolled flat products (SSCR, CN headings 7219 and 7220) from India and Indonesia. Definitive countervailing duties: India Jindal 4.3%, Chromeni and all others 7.5%; Indonesia IRNC Group 21.4%, Jindal Indonesia 0% (de minimis), non-sampled 13.5%, all others 20.5%. Combined countervailing plus anti-dumping up to 42.8% (Chromeni). Indonesia's dominant subsidy was nickel ore for less than adequate remuneration, kept cheap by export bans and the 2009 Mining Law, with cross-border Chinese financing channelled through the Morowali Industrial Park and attributed to the Government of Indonesia (extending the GFF doctrine). Adopted 15 March 2022 (OJ L 88/24). Also amends the parallel anti-dumping Regulation (EU) 2021/2012.
- [The ESAs Review (Regulation (EU) 2019/2175)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2019-2175_esas_review/index.html): the 2019 reform of the three European Supervisory Authorities (EBA, EIOPA, ESMA). Omnibus amending regulation built on Article 114 TFEU. Headline change: EBA becomes the EU anti-money-laundering hub for the entire financial sector (central AML database, internal AML committee, power to request national investigations within 10 working days). New supervisory-convergence tools across all three ESAs (Union strategic supervisory priorities, strengthened peer reviews, public Q&A, no-action letters, whistleblower protection, coordination groups). ESMA gains direct supervision of data reporting services providers (MiFIR) and critical benchmarks (Benchmarks Regulation) from 1 January 2022. Sustainable finance and fintech mandate (ESG risks, Paris Agreement). Amends six regulations. Applied in two waves: Articles 1/2/3/6 from 1 January 2020, Articles 4/5 from 1 January 2022. Contains the textual seed of the later EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) in Article 81.
- [The Animal Health Law (Regulation (EU) 2016/429)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2016-429_animal_health_law/index.html): the single EU framework regulation for transmissible animal diseases, which replaced around 40 prior acts. Adopted 9 March 2016, applied from 21 April 2021. Built on the One Health principle and aligned with the WTO SPS Agreement and World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE/WOAH) standards. Names five diseases directly (foot-and-mouth, classical swine fever, African swine fever, highly pathogenic avian influenza, African horse sickness) and sorts listed diseases into five management categories (A immediate eradication, B compulsory eradication, C optional eradication, D movement restrictions, E surveillance). Covers responsibilities and biosecurity, notification and surveillance, eradication and disease-free status, registration and approval of establishments, identification and traceability, movements and TRACES certification, entry from third countries, non-commercial pet movements (max five pets, EU pet passport) and emergency measures. 283 articles, 9 Parts; three TFEU legal bases (agriculture, internal market, public health).
- [MiCA, the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2023-1114_mica/index.html): the EU's first comprehensive framework for crypto-assets that are not already regulated as financial instruments. Built on Article 114 TFEU under the principle "same activities, same risks, same rules". Classifies crypto into three types: e-money tokens (EMTs, reference one official currency, issuable only by credit or e-money institutions, redeemable at par, no interest), asset-referenced tokens (ARTs, reference a basket or other value, strictest issuer regime with a segregated low-risk reserve and permanent redemption), and other crypto-assets including utility tokens. Issuers must publish a crypto-asset white paper (including the environmental impact of the consensus mechanism); the largest "significant" tokens are supervised directly by the European Banking Authority. Crypto-asset service providers (the ten services: custody, trading platform, exchange for funds or other crypto, execution, placing, reception and transmission of orders, advice, portfolio management, transfer) must be authorised, hold own funds and safeguard client assets, with one EU-wide licence (passporting). ESMA keeps a public register. 149 articles, 9 Titles, 119 recitals. Entered into force 29 June 2023; stablecoin rules (Titles III/IV) apply from 30 June 2024, the rest from 30 December 2024; CASP grandfathering runs to 1 July 2026. Amends the EBA and ESMA regulations, the CRD and the Whistleblower Directive.
- [The AI Act, the Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2024-1689_aiact/index.html): the world's first comprehensive, horizontal law for artificial intelligence, built on Article 114 TFEU under a risk-based approach. Four risk tiers: unacceptable risk (eight prohibited practices in Article 5, including social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, emotion recognition at work and school, and most real-time remote biometric identification by police in public); high risk (Annex I product-safety route plus eight Annex III areas: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential public and private services, law enforcement, migration and asylum, justice and democracy), subject to six mandatory requirements (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency and human oversight, plus accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity), conformity assessment, CE marking and EU-database registration; limited risk (Article 50 transparency duties for chatbots, deepfakes and synthetic content); and minimal risk. A dedicated regime governs general-purpose AI models (technical documentation, a copyright policy honouring the text-and-data-mining opt-out, and a public training-content summary), with extra obligations for models posing systemic risk, presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations. Enforced by a new Union AI Office plus national authorities; fines up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover. 113 articles, 13 Chapters, 180 recitals, 13 Annexes. Entered into force 1 August 2024; prohibitions apply from 2 February 2025, general-purpose-model and governance rules from 2 August 2025, the bulk from 2 August 2026, and product-related high-risk systems from 2 August 2027.
- [Aluminium road wheels from Morocco, countervailing duties (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/500)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2025-500_morocco_aluminium_wheels/index.html): the EU's first anti-subsidy action against Morocco and the fourth application of the cross-border subsidy doctrine. Definitive countervailing duties on certain aluminium road wheels (CN ex 8708 70 10 and ex 8708 70 50): Dika Morocco Africa (DMA) 31.4%, Hands 8 5.6%, all other Morocco 5.6%, on top of the existing anti-dumping duties of 9.0% to 17.5% (Reg 2023/99). Central finding: Chinese Belt-and-Road preferential financing channelled through CITIC Dicastal into its Moroccan subsidiary DMA is attributed to the Government of Morocco as the country of export, applying the doctrine affirmed by the Court of Justice on 28 November 2024 (Hengshi and Jushi Egypt, C-269/23 P and C-272/23 P). DMA's largest single subsidy was a preferential price of inputs (15.65%). The lesser-duty rule does not apply in anti-subsidy cases, so the duty equals the full subsidy amount. Adopted 13 March 2025 under the basic anti-subsidy Regulation (Reg 2016/1037).
- [The Official Controls Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2017/625)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2017-625_official_controls/index.html): the EU's single enforcement framework for the entire agri-food chain, from farm to fork. It does not set substantive standards but harmonises how Member State competent authorities perform official controls and other official activities to verify compliance across ten areas: food and food safety, GMOs for food and feed, feed safety, animal health, animal by-products, animal welfare, plant health, plant protection products and pesticides, organic production, and protected designations of origin, geographical indications and traditional specialities. Covers risk-based unannounced controls, delegation to ISO-accredited bodies, official laboratories accredited to EN ISO/IEC 17025, border control posts with a Common Health Entry Document, mandatory fees at cost or set amounts, EU reference laboratories and centres, the IMSOC computerised system (integrating TRACES and RASFF), multi-annual national control plans, Commission audits, cross-border administrative assistance, whistleblower protection, and effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties (turnover-linked for fraud). 167 articles, 8 Titles, 99 recitals, 5 Annexes. Legal basis Articles 43(2), 114 and 168(4)(b) TFEU. Replaced Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and the meat-controls Regulation (EC) No 854/2004 plus seven Directives and Decisions. Adopted 15 March 2017; entered into force 27 April 2017; applies from 14 December 2019. The companion enforcement instrument to the Animal Health Law.
- [Optical fibre cables from China, anti-dumping duties (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/2011)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2021-2011_optical_fibre_cables/index.html): the EU's anti-dumping action on single-mode optical fibre cables from China (CN ex 8544 70 00), the backbone cable of telecoms and internet networks, and the first anti-dumping (as opposed to anti-subsidy) entry in the Brubru canon. Definitive duties: FiberHome (FTT) group 44.0%, ZTT group 19.7%, other cooperating companies 31.2%, all others 44.0%. Because Chinese domestic prices were found to be distorted, the normal value was constructed under the Article 2(6a) significant-distortions methodology using Argentina as the representative country. The lesser-duty rule applies in anti-dumping, so the duties were set at the dumping margins, which were lower than the injury elimination levels (61.3%, 42.0%, 52.7%). Overall price undercutting was 31.5%. Initiated 24 September 2020 on a Europacable complaint; ran in parallel with a separate anti-subsidy investigation on the same product. Adopted 17 November 2021 under the basic anti-dumping Regulation (Reg 2016/1036).
- [EMA and the Centralised Procedure (Regulation (EC) No 726/2004)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2004-726_ema/index.html): the regulation that established the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the EU centralised marketing authorisation procedure, where one application to the EMA yields one Commission decision valid across the whole Union and EEA. Repealed Regulation (EEC) No 2309/93. CHMP opinion within 210 days (150 days accelerated); marketing authorisation valid 5 years then unlimited; 3-year sunset clause; 8+2+1 (up to 11 years) data and market protection under Article 14(11). Mandatory centralised route for biotech products, orphan medicines, advanced therapies and new active substances for cancer, HIV/AIDS, neurodegenerative disorders, diabetes, auto-immune and viral diseases. The EMA today has 7 scientific committees (CHMP, PRAC, COMP, PDCO, CAT, CVMP, HMPC) and is headquartered in Amsterdam. 90 articles, 5 Titles. The institutional spine of EU medicines law; being replaced by the 2023 pharmaceutical reform (provisional agreement 11 December 2025).
- [Orphan Medicinal Products (Regulation (EC) No 141/2000)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2000-141_orphan/index.html): the EU rare-disease incentive framework, modelled on the US 1983 Orphan Drug Act. Designates a medicine as orphan if it treats a life-threatening or chronically debilitating condition affecting no more than 5 in 10,000 people in the EU (or fails the insufficient-return test) and there is no satisfactory authorised treatment or the product offers significant benefit. Incentives: 10 years of market exclusivity (reducible to 6), protocol assistance, fee waivers and access to the centralised procedure. The orphan exclusivity extends to 12 years if a completed paediatric investigation plan is added (Reg 1901/2006). Designation by the EMA Committee for Orphan Medicinal Products (COMP) within 90 days; Commission decision within 30 days. 11 articles. Implementing rules in Reg (EC) No 847/2000.
- [Clinical Trials Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 536/2014)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2014-536_ctr/index.html): harmonises the authorisation and conduct of clinical trials across the EU through a single application portal (CTIS, the Clinical Trials Information System) and a coordinated assessment led by a reporting Member State. Repealed Directive 2001/20/EC. Two-part assessment report (Part I scientific, jointly assessed, and Part II national/ethical), each 45 days; single decision per Member State in 5 days; tacit authorisation on silence; results summary plus a layperson summary within 1 year of trial end; SUSAR reporting to the EMA within 7 days (fatal/life-threatening) or 15 days; clinical trial master file archived 25 years. Strong subject-protection regime for minors, incapacitated subjects, pregnant or breastfeeding women and emergencies. 99 articles, 19 Chapters, 7 Annexes. Adopted 16 April 2014; became applicable 31 January 2022 once CTIS went live; transition completed 31 January 2025.
- [Advanced Therapy Medicinal Products (Regulation (EC) No 1394/2007)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2007-1394_atmp/index.html): the tailored regime for the most advanced biological medicines: gene therapy medicinal products, somatic cell therapy medicinal products and tissue-engineered products. A lex specialis on Directive 2001/83/EC that makes the EMA centralised procedure mandatory for ATMPs and creates the Committee for Advanced Therapies (CAT), which drafts the scientific opinion for final CHMP approval. Traceability data kept for at least 30 years; scientific-advice fee reductions of 90% for SMEs and 65% for others; ATMP classification recommendation within 60 days; 50% marketing-authorisation fee reduction for hospitals and SMEs. Includes the much-debated hospital exemption (Article 28) for non-routine, single-Member-State, hospital-prepared products. 30 articles, 4 Annexes. Adopted 13 November 2007; applied from 30 December 2008.
- [Paediatric Medicines (Regulation (EC) No 1901/2006)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2006-1901_paediatric/index.html): drives research into medicines for children (the paediatric population, birth to 18 years) through a system of obligations and rewards. Every marketing-authorisation application for a new medicine, and every new indication, form or route of a still-patented medicine, must include the results of an agreed Paediatric Investigation Plan (PIP) or a granted waiver or deferral; assessed by the EMA Paediatric Committee (PDCO) within 60 days. Rewards: a 6-month Supplementary Protection Certificate extension (Article 36, not for orphans), a 2-year extension of orphan market exclusivity from 10 to 12 years (Article 37), and the Paediatric Use Marketing Authorisation (PUMA) for off-patent paediatric medicines (Article 38). 57 articles, 7 Titles. Adopted 12 December 2006; the obligation applies from 26 July 2008. The labelling symbol it foresaw was never introduced; the 2017 ten-year report (COM(2017)626) found gaps in paediatric oncology that fed the 2023 reform.
- [The Community Code (Directive 2001/83/EC)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2001-83_community_code/index.html): the directive half of EU medicines law and a codification of eleven earlier directives (1965 to 1992) into a single Community code for medicinal products for human use. It governs the national, mutual-recognition and decentralised marketing-authorisation procedures, manufacturing and the Qualified Person, labelling and the package leaflet, prescription/non-prescription classification, wholesale distribution, advertising, pharmacovigilance and supervision for medicines outside the centralised EMA route. 130 articles, 14 Titles. Legal base Article 95 TEC. Adopted 6 November 2001 (OJ L 311). As a codification it set no new transposition deadline (Annex II Part B preserves the predecessors' deadlines). Heavily amended since: Dir 2004/27 brought the 8+2+1 data protection and unlimited MA validity, Dir 2004/24 (herbal), Dir 2010/84 + 2012/26 (pharmacovigilance) and Dir 2011/62 (falsified medicines); being replaced by the 2023 pharma reform.
- [Traditional Herbal Medicines (Directive 2004/24/EC)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2004-24_herbal/index.html): amends the Community Code to create a simplified traditional-use registration for herbal medicines that cannot meet the full efficacy bar. Eligibility rests on at least 30 years of documented medicinal use including 15 years within the EU; long use substitutes for clinical-trial efficacy data while full quality and safety requirements remain. Inserts Chapter 2a (Articles 16a to 16i) and creates the EMA Committee for Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC), which issues Community herbal monographs and the EU list of herbal substances. Adopted 31 March 2004 (OJ L 136); transposition deadline 30 October 2005; 7-year transitional period.
- [The Pharmacovigilance Directive (Directive 2010/84/EU)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2010-84_pharmacovigilance/index.html): the directive half of the 2010 pharmacovigilance package (with Regulation (EU) 1235/2010), the biggest EU medicine-safety overhaul since the system began. It rewrote Title IX of the Community Code: marketing-authorisation holders and Member States run audited pharmacovigilance systems; a Qualified Person Responsible for Pharmacovigilance (QPPV) and a pharmacovigilance system master file; risk management plans; the additional-monitoring black triangle; single reporting of suspected adverse reactions to EudraVigilance within 15 days (serious) or 90 days (other); periodic safety update reports reoriented to risk-benefit with single assessment and Union reference dates; signal detection by the new Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee (PRAC); and the urgent Union procedure. Adopted 15 December 2010 (OJ L 348); transposition deadline 21 July 2012.
- [The Falsified Medicines Directive (Directive 2011/62/EU)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2011-62_falsified_medicines/index.html): amends the Community Code to close the legal supply chain to falsified medicines. Defines a falsified medicinal product (false identity, source or history; excludes unintentional quality defects and IP infringements) and introduces mandatory safety features on prescription packs: a unique identifier (2D Data Matrix barcode) and an anti-tampering device, verified at dispensing through the European Medicines Verification System (EMVS). Adds active-substance (API) good-manufacturing-practice and import controls, registration and audit duties, regulation of brokers, and a common EU logo for legal online pharmacies, plus a 24-hour rapid-alert system. Adopted 8 June 2011 (OJ L 174); transposition deadline 2 January 2013; safety features applied from 9 February 2019 under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/161.
- [Pharmacovigilance amendments (Directive 2012/26/EU)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2012-26_pv_amend/index.html): a short follow-up to the 2010 pharmacovigilance package prompted by the benfluorex (Mediator) scandal. It makes the urgent Union safety procedure trigger automatically when a suspension, revocation, non-renewal or supply ban is considered or a new contraindication, dose reduction or indication restriction is needed, and forces marketing-authorisation holders to disclose the reasons for safety-driven withdrawals, including those taken in third countries, with the EMA publishing an annual list with reasons. Adopted 25 October 2012 (OJ L 299); transposition deadline 28 October 2013.
- [European Electronic Communications Code (Directive (EU) 2018/1972)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2018-1972_eecc/index.html): the 2018 recast that merged the four directives of the 2002 telecoms package (Framework, Access, Authorisation, Universal Service) into a single European Electronic Communications Code. Governs general authorisation of networks and services, access and interconnection, market analysis and significant-market-power remedies, the roll-out of very-high-capacity networks and co-investment, radio spectrum (assignment with a minimum 20-year predictability under Article 49 and peer review), end-user rights and universal service, numbering, network security, and the BEREC governance framework. Legal base Article 114 TFEU; adopted 11 December 2018 (OJ L 321); transposition deadline 21 December 2020.
- [Solvency II (Directive 2009/138/EC)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2009-138_solvency2/index.html): the EU risk-based prudential regime for insurers and reinsurers, a recast of fourteen earlier insurance directives, built on three pillars. Pillar 1 (quantitative): market-consistent technical provisions, own funds in three tiers, the Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR) calibrated to a 99.5 percent value-at-risk over one year (Article 101), the Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR), the prudent-person investment principle, and the choice of standard formula or internal model. Pillar 2 (governance): the system of governance, the Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA), fit-and-proper, the supervisory review process and group supervision. Pillar 3 (disclosure): the SFCR and RSR reports. Supervised with EIOPA. Adopted 25 November 2009 (OJ L 335); amended by Omnibus II (2014/51/EU); transposition 31 March 2015, application 1 January 2016.
- [MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2014-65_mifid2/index.html): the recast markets-in-financial-instruments framework, the directive half of the MiFID II / MiFIR package (companion Regulation (EU) No 600/2014). Sets the authorisation and organisational requirements for investment firms, algorithmic and high-frequency trading controls (Article 17), the investor-protection regime (best execution Article 27, suitability and appropriateness Article 25, product governance, the inducements rules, client categorisation), the trading-venue taxonomy (regulated market, MTF and the new organised trading facility, the OTF), SME growth markets, commodity-derivative position limits (Articles 57 to 58), data reporting services, and competent-authority powers and sanctions. Supervised with ESMA. Adopted 15 May 2014 (OJ L 173); the original 3 July 2016 transposition and 3 January 2017 application dates were postponed one year by Directive (EU) 2016/1034, so MiFID II applied from 3 January 2018.
- [Amazon State Aid Decision (Decision (EU) 2018/859)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2018-859_amazon_state_aid/index.html): the Commission's State-aid decision on SA.38944, finding that a Luxembourg advance tax ruling let Amazon route most of its EU profit to a non-taxed limited partnership through an intra-group royalty that departed from the arm's-length principle, a selective advantage and unlawful aid of about EUR 250 million. Legal base Articles 107(1) and 108(2) TFEU. The General Court annulled the decision on 12 May 2021 (T-816/17 and T-318/18) and the Court of Justice dismissed the Commission's appeal on 14 December 2023 (C-457/21 P), so the recovery did not stand. A leading transfer-pricing and tax-ruling State-aid precedent.
- [Apple State Aid Decision (Decision (EU) 2017/1283)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2017-1283_apple_state_aid/index.html): the Commission's State-aid decision on SA.38373, finding that two Irish tax rulings allocated almost all of Apple's sales profit to stateless head offices with no real activity, leaving the Irish branches under-taxed, a selective advantage and unlawful aid of up to about EUR 13 billion plus interest. Legal base Articles 107(1) and 108(2) TFEU. The General Court annulled the decision on 15 July 2020 (T-778/16 and T-892/16) but the Court of Justice set that aside on 10 September 2024 and gave final judgment confirming the Commission (C-465/20 P), so Ireland must recover the aid. The landmark tax-ruling State-aid case.
- [La Rochelle Airport State Aid Decision (Decision (EU) 2023/1683)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2023-1683_la_rochelle_airport/index.html): the Commission's State-aid decision on SA.26494, examining public funding to the operator of La Rochelle airport and the airport-services and marketing agreements with airlines including Ryanair. Applying the market-economy operator principle with an incremental-profitability analysis, it found unlawful aid to the airlines and ordered recovery, assessing airport operating aid under the 2014 Aviation Guidelines. Legal base Articles 107(1) and 108(2) TFEU. A key precedent on airport-airline marketing deals.
- [Nimes Airport State Aid Decision (Decision (EU) 2016/633)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2016-633_nimes_airport/index.html): the Commission's State-aid decision on SA.33961, examining public funding to the managers of Nimes airport and the airport-services and marketing agreements with Ryanair and Airport Marketing Services. Using the market-economy operator test and an incremental-profitability analysis, it found unlawful aid in several agreements and ordered recovery, assessing airport operating aid under the Aviation Guidelines. Legal base Articles 107(1) and 108(2) TFEU. A core regional-airport State-aid precedent.
- [Cineca State Aid Decision (Decision (EU) 2025/1963)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2025-1963_cineca/index.html): the Commission's State-aid decision on SA.39639 concerning the Italian inter-university consortium Cineca and the in-house assignment of public IT and supercomputing services, assessing whether Cineca is an undertaking carrying on economic activity and whether any public-resource advantage distorted competition. Legal base Articles 107(1) and 108(2) TFEU. Clarifies when in-house public-service arrangements stay outside the State-aid rules.
- [NIS2 Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2555)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2022-2555_nis2/index.html): the EU baseline cybersecurity directive, replacing the 2016 NIS1 Directive (repealed 18 October 2024). Brings essential entities and important entities across 18 sectors (Annex I high-criticality: energy, transport, banking, financial market infrastructure, health, drinking water, waste water, digital infrastructure, ICT service management, public administration, space; Annex II other critical: postal, waste management, chemicals, food, manufacturing, digital providers, research) into scope under a size-cap rule. Makes management bodies accountable and obliges training (Article 20), mandates ten minimum cybersecurity risk-management measures including supply-chain security (Article 21), sets a three-stage incident-reporting cascade (early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours, final report within one month, Article 23), and provides for coordinated vulnerability disclosure, the Cooperation Group, the CSIRTs network and EU-CyCLONe. Supervision is differentiated (essential entities ex ante and ex post, important entities ex post), with fines up to EUR 10 million or 2 percent of worldwide turnover for essential entities and EUR 7 million or 1.4 percent for important entities. Legal base Article 114 TFEU; adopted 14 December 2022 (OJ L 333), transposition deadline 17 October 2024. Carries a transposition map of national implementing measures.
- [Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2022-2065_dsa/index.html): the EU horizontal rulebook for online intermediary services. Keeps the conditional liability exemptions for mere conduit, caching and hosting and bans general monitoring obligations, then layers asymmetric due-diligence duties by actor type: all intermediaries, hosting services (notice-and-action, statements of reasons), online platforms (trusted flaggers, ban on dark patterns, advertising transparency, protection of minors, no ads using special-category data, recommender-system transparency, trader traceability), and the extra obligations on Very Large Online Platforms and Search Engines with 45 million plus monthly EU users (systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, independent audits, ad repositories, vetted-researcher data access, crisis response). Enforced by national Digital Services Coordinators and the European Board for Digital Services, with the Commission directly supervising VLOPs and VLOSEs; fines up to 6 percent of total worldwide annual turnover. Legal base Article 114 TFEU; adopted 19 October 2022 (OJ L 277), generally applicable from 17 February 2024.
- [Digital Markets Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/1925)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2022-1925_dma/index.html): the EU ex-ante competition rulebook for large digital platforms. Defines gatekeepers of core platform services (online intermediation, search, social networking, video-sharing, messaging, operating systems, browsers, virtual assistants, cloud, online advertising) by quantitative thresholds (EUR 7.5 billion EEA turnover or EUR 75 billion market cap, 45 million monthly end users and 10,000 yearly business users) with a rebuttable presumption and a market-investigation route. Imposes the Article 5, 6 and 7 obligations: no combining personal data across services without consent, no anti-steering or wide most-favoured-nation clauses, no self-preferencing in ranking, mandatory un-installation and choice screens, interoperability (including number-independent messaging), data portability and real-time access for business users, and FRAND access to app stores. Enforced by the Commission alone with fines up to 10 percent of worldwide turnover, rising to 20 percent for repeated infringements, plus periodic penalty payments and structural remedies. Legal base Article 114 TFEU; adopted 14 September 2022 (OJ L 265), applicable from 2 May 2023.
- [GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2016-679_gdpr/index.html): the EU General Data Protection Regulation, the cornerstone of EU data-protection law. Directly applicable since 25 May 2018 under Article 16 TFEU. Sets the principles of processing (Article 5), the six lawful bases (Article 6), consent (Article 7), special-category data (Article 9), the data-subject rights (transparency, access, rectification, erasure / right to be forgotten, restriction, portability, objection, and rights around automated decisions and profiling, Articles 12 to 22), controller and processor duties (data protection by design and by default, records of processing, the data protection impact assessment Article 35, the data protection officer, security Article 32, and breach notification within 72 hours Articles 33 to 34), international transfers (adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules, Articles 44 to 50), the supervisory authorities, the one-stop-shop and consistency mechanism and the European Data Protection Board (Articles 51 to 76), and the two-tier administrative fines up to EUR 20 million or 4 percent of total worldwide annual turnover (Article 83). Adopted 27 April 2016 (OJ L 119).
- [Tirrenia State Aid Decision (Decision (EU) 2020/1412)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2020-1412_tirrenia/index.html): the Commission's State-aid decision on SA.32014, SA.32015 and SA.32016, assessing public-service compensation for maritime cabotage routes, priority berthing and tax measures granted to Tirrenia, and whether recovery follows to its acquirer Compagnia Italiana di Navigazione through economic continuity. It applied the Altmark conditions and the SGEI framework under Article 106(2) TFEU and found some measures incompatible aid. A leading SGEI, public-service-compensation and economic-continuity precedent.
- [CBAM, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (Regulation (EU) 2023/956)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2023-956_cbam/index.html): the EU's import-side carbon-pricing instrument and the border complement to the EU Emissions Trading System. It is not a tax: importers of covered goods must buy CBAM certificates priced at the weekly average EU ETS auction price, where one certificate equals one tonne of CO2 equivalent, mirroring the carbon cost EU producers bear and designed to be WTO-compatible with no quantitative import limits. Legal base Article 192(1) TFEU, part of the Fit for 55 package. Six covered sectors by CN code: cement, electricity, fertilisers, iron and steel, aluminium and hydrogen (greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide throughout, plus nitrous oxide for fertilisers and perfluorocarbons for aluminium). Two-phase timeline: a transitional reporting-only period from 1 October 2023 to 31 December 2025 (last report due 31 January 2026), then the definitive paying regime from 1 January 2026 with the first annual CBAM declaration for 2026 due 31 May 2027. Only an authorised CBAM declarant may import covered goods; the declarant must hold at least 80 percent of embedded emissions in certificates at each quarter-end, surrender annually by 31 May, may reclaim a carbon price already paid abroad, and benefits from the gradual phase-out of EU ETS free allocation over 2026 to 2034. Penalties mirror the EU ETS excess-emissions penalty, rising three to five times for non-declarant importers. Exempt origins: Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland and the territories of Büsingen, Heligoland, Livigno, Ceuta and Melilla. 36 articles, 116 recitals, 11 chapters, 6 annexes. Adopted 10 May 2023 (OJ L 130), in force 17 May 2023, with scope set to expand toward all EU ETS sectors by 2030.
- [DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2022-2554_dora/index.html): the EU's first horizontal cybersecurity rulebook for the financial sector. Directly applicable from 17 January 2025 under Article 114 TFEU and lex specialis vs the NIS 2 Directive. Covers around 22,000 financial entities across 21 categories (credit institutions, payment institutions, e-money institutions, account information service providers, investment firms, crypto-asset service providers and asset-referenced token issuers, CSDs, CCPs, trading venues, trade repositories, AIFMs, UCITS management companies, data reporting service providers, insurers and reinsurers, insurance intermediaries, IORPs, credit rating agencies, critical benchmark administrators, crowdfunding service providers, securitisation repositories) plus ICT third-party service providers. Five pillars (ICT risk management, ICT-related incident reporting, digital operational resilience testing including threat-led penetration testing every 3 years and aligned with TIBER-EU, ICT third-party risk management with mandatory contractual provisions and a register of information, voluntary information-sharing arrangements) plus a Union-level Oversight Framework run by Lead Overseers from EBA, ESMA or EIOPA for critical ICT third-party service providers, with periodic penalty payments up to 1 percent of average daily worldwide turnover for non-cooperation and a 12-month deadline for third-country CTPPs to set up a Union subsidiary. Companion Directive (EU) 2022/2556 amends UCITS, Solvency II, AIFMD, CRD IV, BRRD, MiFID II, PSD2 and IORP II. 64 articles, 106 recitals, 9 Chapters, 65 definitions. Adopted 14 December 2022 (OJ L 333), in force 16 January 2023, applies from 17 January 2025 with a full review by 17 January 2028.
- [EHDS, the European Health Data Space (Regulation (EU) 2025/327)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2025-327_ehds/index.html): the first sector-specific European data space, giving every natural person in the Union six substantive rights over their personal electronic health data (access, insertion, rectification, portability, restriction of access, information on any access) in six priority categories for primary use (patient summaries, electronic prescriptions, electronic dispensations, medical imaging studies and reports, medical test results, discharge reports, main characteristics in Annex I). Two cross-border infrastructures: MyHealth@EU (Chapter II Section 3) links national contact points for digital health so that every healthcare provider and every pharmacy in the Union can exchange the priority categories and dispense electronic prescriptions issued in another Member State; HealthData@EU (Chapter IV Section 4) links national health data access bodies for secondary use across 17 minimum data categories (Article 51, from EHR records through genetic and omics data to biobanks) restricted to 6 permitted purposes (Article 53: public health, policymaking, statistics, education, scientific research including AI training, care improvement) and 5 prohibited uses (Article 54: detrimental decisions, discrimination in employment or insurance or credit, advertising or marketing, harmful products, unethical activities). Chapter III turns EHR systems into CE-marked products with two mandatory harmonised software components (European interoperability + European logging, Annex II) verified through a European digital testing environment. Wellness applications that claim interoperability with EHR systems carry a label valid for a maximum of three years. Article 71 gives every natural person an unconditional reversible right to opt out from secondary use. Fines are up to EUR 10 million or 2 percent of worldwide turnover for holder or user duty breaches (Article 64(4)) and up to EUR 20 million or 4 percent for re-identification or extraction from secure processing environments (Article 64(5)). Amends Directive 2011/24/EU (Article 14 on the eHealth Network deleted from 26 March 2031) and Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act) to align conformity assessment. 105 articles, 115 recitals, 9 Chapters, 4 Annexes. Legal base Articles 16 and 114 TFEU. Adopted 11 February 2025 at Strasbourg (OJ L, 2025/327, 5.3.2025), in force 25 March 2025; general application 26 March 2027; Chapter IV (secondary use) from 26 March 2029; Chapter III (EHR systems) and priority categories d/e/f from 26 March 2031; third-country participation in HealthData@EU from 26 March 2035.
- [PPWR, the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2025/40)](https://brubru.beresol.eu/eucanon/2025-40_ppwr/index.html): the first EU-wide horizontal packaging law binding directly on economic operators, repealing Directive 94/62/EC after 30 years. 13 Chapters, 71 Articles, 13 Annexes, 189 recitals. Sets sustainability requirements for every packaging placed on the Union market: from 12 August 2026 restricts per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in food-contact packaging above 25 ppb any single PFAS, 250 ppb sum, 50 ppm PFAS-total; keeps the 100 mg/kg sum limit on lead, cadmium, mercury and hexavalent chromium. From 1 January 2030 every packaging must be recyclable and classified into Grades A, B or C per Annex II Table 3, with Grade C losing market access from 1 January 2038. Minimum recycled-content targets on plastic packaging by 2030 (contact-sensitive PET 30 percent, other contact-sensitive plastic 10 percent, single-use plastic beverage bottles 30 percent, other plastic 35 percent) and by 2040 (50, 25, 65 and 65 percent). Empty-space ratio ceiling of 50 percent for grouped, transport and e-commerce packaging from 1 January 2030. Annex V bans single-use packaging formats in the hospitality sector (single-serve condiment, sauce, cream and sugar sachets; single-use hotel amenities under 100 ml or 100 g), fruit and vegetable pre-packs under 1.5 kg, shrink wrap for luggage at airports, and very lightweight plastic carrier bags under 15 microns except for hygiene or loose-food wastage prevention. Sector-specific reuse targets by 2030 (with 2040 uplifts): transport packaging 40 percent (70), large white goods 90 percent (100), pallet wraps and straps 30 percent (70), take-away cold or hot beverages 10 percent (40). Article 34 caps lightweight plastic carrier bags at 40 per capita per year by 31 December 2025. Deposit Return Systems must reach 90 percent separate collection of single-use PET beverage bottles and aluminium beverage cans up to 3 litres by 1 January 2029, with a derogation route for Member States already at 80 percent by end 2026. Modernises Extended Producer Responsibility with fee modulation based on Grade A/B/C. Amends the Single-Use Plastics Directive (2019/904) to add multi-pack plastic rings, shrink wrap for luggage and expanded-polystyrene chips to the SUP restriction list, and amends the Market Surveillance Regulation (2019/1020). Green public procurement rules under Article 63 (Commission implementing act by 12 February 2030) bind contracting authorities where packaging exceeds 30 percent of contract value. Legal base Article 114 TFEU. Adopted 19 December 2024, published in OJ L, 2025/40, 22 January 2025, in force 11 February 2025; general application 12 August 2026; penalties framework by 12 February 2027; Commission evaluation by 12 August 2034.

## Subscription Plans

Brubru offers a 14-day free trial. There is no permanent free tier. Annual billing is also available on each plan.

- Starter (EUR 39/month): AI Chat with the full knowledge base + My EU Bubble dashboard with RSS aggregation and legislative tracking
- Advocate (EUR 59/month): Everything in Starter plus Amendator (Akoma Ntoso XML), AI amendment suggestions, and PDF/Word/HTML exports
- Professional (EUR 99/month): Complete platform - adds EU Law Comply (compliance gap analysis), Tenderator (TED tender intelligence), unlimited AI Predictions, Council QMV analysis, and dedicated support
- EP Plan (EUR 49/month): Tailored for accredited parliamentary assistants and MEPs with EP-specific AI context
- Enterprise (custom pricing): Multi-user accounts, SSO, white-label and on-premise options. Contact hello@beresol.eu
